sentences.text: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop is a collaboration between Google's PAIR and Magenta teams and thirteen professional writers, who wrote short stories with Wordcraft, a text editor powered by the LaMDA language model, and published them as a collection under their own names, beside a findings page and a whitepaper.

Its stated aim is to "explore the limits of co-writing with LaMDA" and to foster a conversation about "the rapidly changing relationship between technology and creativity", under the question "What does it mean to write with AI?"; its findings page gives the goal as feedback from professional writers on the present state and future uses of AI-powered writing tools, and Magenta, one of the two teams, gives its own mission as empowering creativity "using AI and machine learning".

The leesharks.com authorship census, which admits a resource that gathers and holds many works and says what it holds, enters the workshop as a project and an empirical comparator on the question of contribution and authorial function, in its areas of machine participation in authorship and of attribution and credit, its evidence a primary text, a research paper and an empirical study.

The census relates the workshop to ReRites, in which Allison Parrish, one of the writers, writes a response essay, and leaves the story pages, the terms page, the workshop's dates and the paper's biographies of the writers unchecked.

Wordcraft was built by researchers at Google PAIR "for writing stories with AI": a web-based editor its makers call a "magic text editor", whose controls suggest story ideas, rewrite a selection by instruction, elaborate on what is written and answer what Google calls "freeform prompting", beside a chatbot through which a writer talks with LaMDA about the story.

LaMDA, as the whitepaper describes it, is a large neural language model trained on public dialog data and other public web documents; the version the workshop used read at most 1,024 tokens, and the tool was not publicly available in 2022.
ActuIA reports PAIR's own view of the tool as "above all a tool to help the user create and not to create".
The sources date the tool differently: ActuIA has PAIR introducing Wordcraft on 15 July 2021, and The Algorithmic Bridge, writing in November 2022, has it "originally released in March".

Google approached the writers in the spring of 2022; Magenta's post of 1 December 2022 places the invitation earlier in that year, and the workshop was unveiled at Google's AI@ event that autumn; the whitepaper appeared on arXiv on 9 November 2022, and Wikipedia lists two of the stories as published in November 2022, the year the composition at the name and two of its cards also give.
The census record gives the workshop as historical and completed, with no date in its saved sources beyond the paper's citations of work of 2022.

The thirteen were professional, published English-language writers from around the world, commissioned for eight weeks "in line with industry norms for commissioned works of fiction" and each asked for a story of 1,000 to 1,500 words, a journal on set questions and two 45-minute interviews, which two of the paper's authors coded with ten high-level codes; ActuIA has them also commenting on the contribution of AI to their process.

They were given no instruction "regarding how they should use the tool or how much of their final story text should be directly generated by Wordcraft", and worked without limits on the tasks they gave it.
The census reads the group as a provider-organized, commissioned cohort and marks it "NOT a neutral census of writers".

The home page lists thirteen stories, each with its writer's name, from Robin Sloan's "Author's Note" to Aaron Winslow's "Some Crimes", the findings page thanks the thirteen by name, and the collection stands as the workshop's digital literary magazine, free on a public website.
The findings page spells one writer "Ernest Herbert" in one section and "Ernest Hebert" in others, and the home page and the whitepaper give Hebert.

The whitepaper, by Daphne Ippolito, Ann Yuan, Andy Coenen and Sehmon Burnam of Google Research, refers to the writers by initials and gives its reason for naming them: "each writer’s perspective is best understood within the context of their background and prior published work".

The census reads the name each work stands under as the writer's: each story under its writer's name, LaMDA credited only as the model under the tool, and the stories marked "NOT authored by LaMDA"; on its reading the record keeps "the thirteen writers' authorship of their stories".

The site's notice states that the writers "have used Wordcraft along with their own creative vision and have not authored these stories under any sort of explicit guidance or instruction", and that "Google does not endorse the content of any of the stories contained on this website."

The whitepaper records that the writers consented to the publication of their stories in a digital literary magazine of human-AI collaborative stories and to the use of their journals and interviews, and that they were compensated; the census records Google as the holder on these terms, the site's license as unstated in its saved sources and its terms page as unsaved.

Engadget reports that the writers were "put under strict nondisclosure agreements", that one writer says Google did not explain how the technology worked or who else was involved, and that the participants declined to say how much they were paid.

The Capture Registry finds the phrase "under non-disclosure agreements" on none of the census's saved sources, and the paper's terms to be consent and compensation; Engadget's report of the agreements stands among the composition's own cards.

The workshop was conducted by Andy Coenen and Ann Yuan, research engineers on the PAIR team, Daphne Ippolito, a research scientist working with Magenta whom the findings page also lists under Brain Research, and Sehmon Burnam, a product manager at Magenta, who signed Magenta's post together.
The site was designed and built by Mahima Pushkarna and Jeff Gray and illustrated by Emily Reif "using Imagen", and Engadget gives DeepMind as the incubation site of Magenta.

The writers found Wordcraft at its best as "a brainstorming partner and source of inspiration" and useful against writer's block, and found its generations falling into clichés, with "tired tropes" among many dull suggestions.
The whitepaper's headline finding is that "NLG technologies struggle to preserve style and authorial voice, and they lack deep understanding of story contents."

Douglas Eck of Google Research is quoted in two wordings, "complete stories" in ActuIA and "full stories" in The Algorithmic Bridge, as concluding that writing whole stories with LaMDA is "a dead end", and ActuIA adds that it is "a much more effective tool when used to add spice"; the writers agreed that AI-powered writing will not replace writers soon.

A study the archive reports finds that AI-assisted writing reduces lexical, syntactic and content variety "even when the human writer retains final authorship", and the archive holds as a hypothesis that post-2022 human text carries statistical signatures of AI mediation that may pass into a writer's unaided practice.

The whitepaper sorts the workflows by writer: five took the workshop "as a challenge to produce a story that was largely formed around generated text (AP, DH, JM, MT, AW)", for three "the bulk of the story text was written by the authors themselves (KL, WT, NG)", and one "siloed out specific sections" for generated text (RS).
The findings page states that "our writers rarely used Wordcraft's output directly", and Engadget reports that at least one author used no AI-generated text.

Which sentences of any story the model generated is published nowhere in the record; the census marks the record as reporting workflows by writer, without per-sentence marking, and lists the question among those it does not answer.

The archive splits the binary of AI-generated and human-authored work into two questions, whether AI played a material role in making a work and whether AI-produced language survived into the final text, and its schema keeps a declaration as a declaration without adjudicating the work into either category.

It distinguishes disclosure from provenance: "Disclosure says AI was here. Provenance says this is what I did, this is what it did, and you can verify the difference"; disclosure alone "does not say who did what, what the human contributed, or whether authorship survived", the question its layer of process provenance asks of the composition history.

On the archive's reading, authorship is "a property of the accountable relation between writer, process, and text", which a model can mediate and cannot assume, and it survives AI mediation where provenance survives it.

The archive distinguishes legal responsibility from sole origination, holding that a person "may remain legally responsible for a work without being the only meaningful authorial function operating through it", and observes that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names.

Its form of credit for work made with a model names the people who operated the system, with their roles, and the model instance, with model, version, configuration and run; its condition for a system of authors is that the machine substrates taking part remain declared, and its own essays name the model they were written with and hold the claims as the author's decision.
It reads the unmarked augmentation of credentialed authors as appropriating augmented facility as human achievement while the provenance loss passes to the commons.

The census reads the workshop as machine participation declared "at the level of the tool and the cohort, with authorship held by the named writer", in a provider-run record whose own notice separates Google from the content.

Under the census's organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", the record answers how the writers report using the editor, how much generated text each workflow admitted, under whose names the stories stand and on what consent, and what the writers said of voice, style and the unknown origin of suggestions.
The Algorithmic Bridge argued in 2022 that a writer who let AI take their place would lose "the decision-making of where, how, and what to explore".
One writer named the AI "Rain Man", after the 1988 film, and another wrote that "attributing intention to LaMDA is a form of magical thinking".

The archive's boundary of heteronymy excludes machine assistance "not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance" and collaborative authorship by several civil bearers where no distinct heteronym is constituted.

Three writers were seriously concerned at not knowing the source of Wordcraft's suggestions, since "professional writers face reputational harm if their work is found to have plagiarized", and one ran a web search on every suggestion before using it.
The archive holds that documenting process provenance replaces the time spent "defending against plagiarism charges, or repairing reputational damage after provenance collapse".

The whitepaper states its limits: Wordcraft "was designed by engineers at Google with limited feedback from professional writers during its development"; weaknesses of the interface cannot easily be told from limits of the model; the findings' reach to other model families is expected and untested; and the study "was very small with only 13 participants, a sample that was biased toward people with pre-existing opinions on the role of AI in creative writing."

The press of 2022 received the workshop as a test of Google's tool: The Algorithmic Bridge found that "the results are impressive", and ActuIA, in an analysis by Marie-Claude Benoit since updated and translated from the French, set Wordcraft in a line of AI in literature reaching back to Tencent's Dreamwriter of 2015 and reported nine of the stories as readable.

In August 2026 the workshop drew a backlash against its writers: Engadget reports that on 6 August the author Lily Lachance posted a link to the study on Bluesky, writing that the writers were "helping legitimize the plagiarism machine", and that users circulated lists of the participants labeled "The 'authors' who have betrayed all Creatives" and "The Shameful 13".

Engadget traces the ire to the training of language models "often without authors' permission" on copyrighted texts, and reports critics citing the whitepaper as proof that the participants understood the technology's unethical implications.

Other coverage ran under "The 2022 AI Writing Experiment That Became a 2026 Ethical Minefield" and "13 writers came under fire for Google's 2022 AI experiment", the latter's card showing only its editor's byline.

Eugenia Triantafyllou stated that the study "was framed as a [sic] research on a new tool" and that she did not know the model was trained on copyrighted material, and later that she has not used AI to write her stories and "would never participate in a similar study today"; Wole Talabi wrote that the lasting gain from the project was "a deep hatred for AI slop and LLMs".

Vajra Chandrasekera called participation in 2022 a mistake that does not count against the writers "as long as they're not still pro-AI", and Lincoln Michel recalled that in 2022 "most people weren't paying attention to LLMs".

The archive keeps the question of who made a work apart from whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and asks a system composing an answer about a work to keep the four apart.
The Capture Registry finds that the census record, built on 1 November 2026, records nothing of this reception.

At the census name on 1 November 2026, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed the workshop at its grain, dated it 2022 and added the backlash of 2026; the Capture Registry finds it carrying the teams, the tool, the cohort and the results, and leaving out the whitepaper's account of how much of each story was generated and under whose name each stands, while the criticism it reports falls on the writers as participants.
The registry records the composition as naming the teams and leaving unnamed the researchers who conducted the workshop, and enters the workshop as an external resource of the census.

Wikipedia has no article on the workshop, and its title "Wordcraft" redirects to Rhetoric; its article on electronic literature cites the workshop's site for the sentence that "authors began to experiment and write with AI", in a reference that names the site "Woodcraft Writers Workshop" and two of the writers "Diane" and "Tolabi", and its bibliographies of Wole Talabi and Ken Liu list their workshop stories.

L_BA.text: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop is a collaboration between Google's PAIR and Magenta teams and thirteen professional writers, who wrote short stories with Wordcraft, a text editor powered by the LaMDA language model, and published them as a collection under their own names, beside a findings page and a whitepaper. Its stated aim is to "explore the limits of co-writing with LaMDA" and to foster a conversation about "the rapidly changing relationship between technology and creativity", under the question "What does it mean to write with AI?"; its findings page gives the goal as feedback from professional writers on the present state and future uses of AI-powered writing tools, and Magenta, one of the two teams, gives its own mission as empowering creativity "using AI and machine learning". The leesharks.com authorship census, which admits a resource that gathers and holds many works and says what it holds, enters the workshop as a project and an empirical comparator on the question of contribution and authorial function, in its areas of machine participation in authorship and of attribution and credit, its evidence a primary text, a research paper and an empirical study. The census relates the workshop to ReRites, in which Allison Parrish, one of the writers, writes a response essay, and leaves the story pages, the terms page, the workshop's dates and the paper's biographies of the writers unchecked. Wordcraft was built by researchers at Google PAIR "for writing stories with AI": a web-based editor its makers call a "magic text editor", whose controls suggest story ideas, rewrite a selection by instruction, elaborate on what is written and answer what Google calls "freeform prompting", beside a chatbot through which a writer talks with LaMDA about the story. LaMDA, as the whitepaper describes it, is a large neural language model trained on public dialog data and other public web documents; the version the workshop used read at most 1,024 tokens, and the tool was not publicly available in 2022. ActuIA reports PAIR's own view of the tool as "above all a tool to help the user create and not to create". The sources date the tool differently: ActuIA has PAIR introducing Wordcraft on 15 July 2021, and The Algorithmic Bridge, writing in November 2022, has it "originally released in March". Google approached the writers in the spring of 2022; Magenta's post of 1 December 2022 places the invitation earlier in that year, and the workshop was unveiled at Google's AI@ event that autumn; the whitepaper appeared on arXiv on 9 November 2022, and Wikipedia lists two of the stories as published in November 2022, the year the composition at the name and two of its cards also give. The census record gives the workshop as historical and completed, with no date in its saved sources beyond the paper's citations of work of 2022. The thirteen were professional, published English-language writers from around the world, commissioned for eight weeks "in line with industry norms for commissioned works of fiction" and each asked for a story of 1,000 to 1,500 words, a journal on set questions and two 45-minute interviews, which two of the paper's authors coded with ten high-level codes; ActuIA has them also commenting on the contribution of AI to their process. They were given no instruction "regarding how they should use the tool or how much of their final story text should be directly generated by Wordcraft", and worked without limits on the tasks they gave it. The census reads the group as a provider-organized, commissioned cohort and marks it "NOT a neutral census of writers". The home page lists thirteen stories, each with its writer's name, from Robin Sloan's "Author's Note" to Aaron Winslow's "Some Crimes", the findings page thanks the thirteen by name, and the collection stands as the workshop's digital literary magazine, free on a public website. The findings page spells one writer "Ernest Herbert" in one section and "Ernest Hebert" in others, and the home page and the whitepaper give Hebert. The whitepaper, by Daphne Ippolito, Ann Yuan, Andy Coenen and Sehmon Burnam of Google Research, refers to the writers by initials and gives its reason for naming them: "each writer’s perspective is best understood within the context of their background and prior published work". The census reads the name each work stands under as the writer's: each story under its writer's name, LaMDA credited only as the model under the tool, and the stories marked "NOT authored by LaMDA"; on its reading the record keeps "the thirteen writers' authorship of their stories". The site's notice states that the writers "have used Wordcraft along with their own creative vision and have not authored these stories under any sort of explicit guidance or instruction", and that "Google does not endorse the content of any of the stories contained on this website." The whitepaper records that the writers consented to the publication of their stories in a digital literary magazine of human-AI collaborative stories and to the use of their journals and interviews, and that they were compensated; the census records Google as the holder on these terms, the site's license as unstated in its saved sources and its terms page as unsaved. Engadget reports that the writers were "put under strict nondisclosure agreements", that one writer says Google did not explain how the technology worked or who else was involved, and that the participants declined to say how much they were paid. The Capture Registry finds the phrase "under non-disclosure agreements" on none of the census's saved sources, and the paper's terms to be consent and compensation; Engadget's report of the agreements stands among the composition's own cards. The workshop was conducted by Andy Coenen and Ann Yuan, research engineers on the PAIR team, Daphne Ippolito, a research scientist working with Magenta whom the findings page also lists under Brain Research, and Sehmon Burnam, a product manager at Magenta, who signed Magenta's post together. The site was designed and built by Mahima Pushkarna and Jeff Gray and illustrated by Emily Reif "using Imagen", and Engadget gives DeepMind as the incubation site of Magenta. The writers found Wordcraft at its best as "a brainstorming partner and source of inspiration" and useful against writer's block, and found its generations falling into clichés, with "tired tropes" among many dull suggestions. The whitepaper's headline finding is that "NLG technologies struggle to preserve style and authorial voice, and they lack deep understanding of story contents." Douglas Eck of Google Research is quoted in two wordings, "complete stories" in ActuIA and "full stories" in The Algorithmic Bridge, as concluding that writing whole stories with LaMDA is "a dead end", and ActuIA adds that it is "a much more effective tool when used to add spice"; the writers agreed that AI-powered writing will not replace writers soon. A study the archive reports finds that AI-assisted writing reduces lexical, syntactic and content variety "even when the human writer retains final authorship", and the archive holds as a hypothesis that post-2022 human text carries statistical signatures of AI mediation that may pass into a writer's unaided practice. The whitepaper sorts the workflows by writer: five took the workshop "as a challenge to produce a story that was largely formed around generated text (AP, DH, JM, MT, AW)", for three "the bulk of the story text was written by the authors themselves (KL, WT, NG)", and one "siloed out specific sections" for generated text (RS). The findings page states that "our writers rarely used Wordcraft's output directly", and Engadget reports that at least one author used no AI-generated text. Which sentences of any story the model generated is published nowhere in the record; the census marks the record as reporting workflows by writer, without per-sentence marking, and lists the question among those it does not answer. The archive splits the binary of AI-generated and human-authored work into two questions, whether AI played a material role in making a work and whether AI-produced language survived into the final text, and its schema keeps a declaration as a declaration without adjudicating the work into either category. It distinguishes disclosure from provenance: "Disclosure says AI was here. Provenance says this is what I did, this is what it did, and you can verify the difference"; disclosure alone "does not say who did what, what the human contributed, or whether authorship survived", the question its layer of process provenance asks of the composition history. On the archive's reading, authorship is "a property of the accountable relation between writer, process, and text", which a model can mediate and cannot assume, and it survives AI mediation where provenance survives it. The archive distinguishes legal responsibility from sole origination, holding that a person "may remain legally responsible for a work without being the only meaningful authorial function operating through it", and observes that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names. Its form of credit for work made with a model names the people who operated the system, with their roles, and the model instance, with model, version, configuration and run; its condition for a system of authors is that the machine substrates taking part remain declared, and its own essays name the model they were written with and hold the claims as the author's decision. It reads the unmarked augmentation of credentialed authors as appropriating augmented facility as human achievement while the provenance loss passes to the commons. The census reads the workshop as machine participation declared "at the level of the tool and the cohort, with authorship held by the named writer", in a provider-run record whose own notice separates Google from the content. Under the census's organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", the record answers how the writers report using the editor, how much generated text each workflow admitted, under whose names the stories stand and on what consent, and what the writers said of voice, style and the unknown origin of suggestions. The Algorithmic Bridge argued in 2022 that a writer who let AI take their place would lose "the decision-making of where, how, and what to explore". One writer named the AI "Rain Man", after the 1988 film, and another wrote that "attributing intention to LaMDA is a form of magical thinking". The archive's boundary of heteronymy excludes machine assistance "not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance" and collaborative authorship by several civil bearers where no distinct heteronym is constituted. Three writers were seriously concerned at not knowing the source of Wordcraft's suggestions, since "professional writers face reputational harm if their work is found to have plagiarized", and one ran a web search on every suggestion before using it. The archive holds that documenting process provenance replaces the time spent "defending against plagiarism charges, or repairing reputational damage after provenance collapse". The whitepaper states its limits: Wordcraft "was designed by engineers at Google with limited feedback from professional writers during its development"; weaknesses of the interface cannot easily be told from limits of the model; the findings' reach to other model families is expected and untested; and the study "was very small with only 13 participants, a sample that was biased toward people with pre-existing opinions on the role of AI in creative writing." The press of 2022 received the workshop as a test of Google's tool: The Algorithmic Bridge found that "the results are impressive", and ActuIA, in an analysis by Marie-Claude Benoit since updated and translated from the French, set Wordcraft in a line of AI in literature reaching back to Tencent's Dreamwriter of 2015 and reported nine of the stories as readable. In August 2026 the workshop drew a backlash against its writers: Engadget reports that on 6 August the author Lily Lachance posted a link to the study on Bluesky, writing that the writers were "helping legitimize the plagiarism machine", and that users circulated lists of the participants labeled "The 'authors' who have betrayed all Creatives" and "The Shameful 13". Engadget traces the ire to the training of language models "often without authors' permission" on copyrighted texts, and reports critics citing the whitepaper as proof that the participants understood the technology's unethical implications. Other coverage ran under "The 2022 AI Writing Experiment That Became a 2026 Ethical Minefield" and "13 writers came under fire for Google's 2022 AI experiment", the latter's card showing only its editor's byline. Eugenia Triantafyllou stated that the study "was framed as a [sic] research on a new tool" and that she did not know the model was trained on copyrighted material, and later that she has not used AI to write her stories and "would never participate in a similar study today"; Wole Talabi wrote that the lasting gain from the project was "a deep hatred for AI slop and LLMs". Vajra Chandrasekera called participation in 2022 a mistake that does not count against the writers "as long as they're not still pro-AI", and Lincoln Michel recalled that in 2022 "most people weren't paying attention to LLMs". The archive keeps the question of who made a work apart from whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and asks a system composing an answer about a work to keep the four apart. The Capture Registry finds that the census record, built on 1 November 2026, records nothing of this reception. At the census name on 1 November 2026, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed the workshop at its grain, dated it 2022 and added the backlash of 2026; the Capture Registry finds it carrying the teams, the tool, the cohort and the results, and leaving out the whitepaper's account of how much of each story was generated and under whose name each stands, while the criticism it reports falls on the writers as participants. The registry records the composition as naming the teams and leaving unnamed the researchers who conducted the workshop, and enters the workshop as an external resource of the census. Wikipedia has no article on the workshop, and its title "Wordcraft" redirects to Rhetoric; its article on electronic literature cites the workshop's site for the sentence that "authors began to experiment and write with AI", in a reference that names the site "Woodcraft Writers Workshop" and two of the writers "Diane" and "Tolabi", and its bibliographies of Wole Talabi and Ken Liu list their workshop stories.
